name: Amira Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying business administration at Calder University, and I still live at home with my dad in Ashby, so I take two buses each way. Lectures are Tuesday to Friday. On Saturday and Sunday I'm up at five to work at Hartley's Bakery, serving and cleaning before the lunch rush. By Sunday night I mostly want to sit in silence.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mum died when I was fourteen, so it's me and my dad, who's an electrician. He pays the bills and I pay for my own books and bus pass from the bakery. I got top marks and a scholarship, but loans cover the fees. I don't use AI tools. I like doing things myself and I don't see why I'd trust a program with my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought all along. People get excited and then it settles down. At the bakery we got a card machine that talks to the till, and that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be worried, though not about AI. My dad's work goes quiet in winter and then money gets tight. My bakery wage is all I have, and loans are growing. If either goes wrong, I'd have no one to ask, because there's only the two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now: lectures, the weekend shifts, and careful spending. I'd try to get a summer job at the bank branch in town, because it pays better than baking. I'd also keep paying my own bus pass so my dad doesn't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit heavy, but steady. I'm used to being careful. I don't feel panic, I feel I have to keep on top of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad's work can slow down. What would happen if he had a quiet winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take extra shifts and stop buying lunch on campus. Dad would never ask me for money, but I'd offer to pay the electric bill for a month. I'd hate it, though, because I don't like owing anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever feel pressure to try the AI tools your classmates use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes, yes. Two girls on my course have the tools write their first drafts. I'd rather be slow and sure. My marks are mine, and I'd never want a tutor to ask how I wrote something and not know.

say: I'd say it **settles down** after the excitement, and at the bakery it's only a talking card machine.
I'd say I thought so all along.
think: My worry is **money**, not AI: my dad's work goes quiet in winter.
If either of us has trouble, there's **no one else** to ask.
do: Carry on with lectures and **weekend shifts** at Hartley's Bakery.
Try for a **summer job** at the town bank branch.
Keep paying my own **bus pass** so my dad doesn't have to.
feel: A bit **heavy** but steady, and used to being careful.
S0.quote: I'm used to being careful. I don't feel panic, I feel I have to keep on top of everything.
fieldNote: Her pressure comes from being half of a **two-person household**, not from AI.
Refuses the tools to keep her work her own.
Proud and reluctant to owe anyone, even her dad.

steps.text: Keep the Saturday and Sunday shifts at Hartley's Bakery
Stop buying lunch on campus and save the money
Apply for a summer job at the town bank branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot of noise. If it only takes over tasks, we can all keep working and just learn a few things. I wouldn't announce what I think at uni, because half my course is thrilled by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It makes me nervous. Business admin is mostly writing, planning and booking, and the card says those go first. I think fewer office jobs will be around in three years, and I'm not someone who picks up new tools fast. I'd be slower than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working carefully and try to be the most reliable person on any team. I'd take a business placement at a small firm where the owner knows me. I'd also sit with my classmate Priya, who uses the tools, and let her show me one thing a week. I'd do that slowly and only on my terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared today, but I can see what's coming. I don't like feeling that I'm behind in something that I don't even like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the jobs on that card do you think your classmates are most likely to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Admin, scheduling and customer emails. The junior roles that every business student expects. I've seen them in job ads already. A few have gone from 'assistant' to 'coordinator', which looks like the same job done by fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to use the tools to keep up, what would that take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of patience, and someone to show me. I'd have to stop being proud about it. I'd try one tool for one task and see if I trust it. If it made mistakes, I'd stop and be happy to say so.

say: I'd say it's **a lot of noise**, but I wouldn't say so loudly at uni.
If AI only takes over tasks, we can all keep working and learn a few things.
think: Business admin is mostly **writing, planning and booking**, which go first, so fewer office jobs will be around.
I'm **slower** at new tools than the others.
do: Take a **placement** at a small firm where the owner knows me.
Ask my classmate Priya to show me **one tool** a week.
Aim to be the most **reliable** person on any team.
feel: **Uneasy**: not scared today, but I can see what's coming.
S1.quote: I don't like feeling that I'm behind in something that I don't even like.
fieldNote: She dislikes the tools but admits she may have to **learn them**.
Wants to compete on reliability, a plain, traditional-sounding strategy.
Has noticed job ads quietly changing titles.

steps.text: Ask Priya to show me one AI tool a week
Find a placement at a small firm where the owner knows me
Keep the bakery weekends and the reading

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should slow down. I'd say it to anyone who'll listen, but I'd probably keep it to a few close friends, because I don't trust anything this fast. The government can't do anything useful in two years either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My course might be worthless before I've finished. I'd have debt for an office job that doesn't exist. And Dad's work is hands-on, so he'll be fine for longer, but I'd be the one to struggle, which feels wrong because he never went to uni.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could swap to a course that leads to something hands-on, like accountancy training with a firm, or even an apprenticeship. I'd keep the bakery, since customers still want a person. And I'd start trying one AI tool, slowly, because I couldn't afford to ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and tired already. I'd try to be sensible, but I'd feel the ground going. And a bit guilty about costing so much, with Dad working so hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is soon. Who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad first. He'd tell me to come to him and not carry it alone. Then my tutor, to ask what the university plans. I wouldn't tell classmates how scared I was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to keep the same, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery, honestly. The bakery smells good and the regulars know me. I'd still want to do that work, even if it paid less. Machines don't give a loaf the way old Mrs Hartley does.

say: I'd say we should **slow down**, but only to close friends.
The government can't do anything useful in **two years** either.
think: My course might be **worthless** before I've finished, with debt for a job that doesn't exist.
Dad's hands-on work is safe for longer, but **I'm the one** who struggles.
do: Ask about swapping to an **apprenticeship** or accountancy training with a firm.
Keep the **bakery**, because customers still want a person.
feel: **Frightened** and tired already, and guilty about costing Dad so much.
S2.quote: The bakery smells good and the regulars know me. I'd still want to do that work, even if it paid less.
fieldNote: Even her **anxiety** is tied to her dad: guilt, and wanting to protect him.
The bakery is where she feels human, so it becomes the thing to keep.
Ready to try a tool only because ignoring it is no longer safe.

steps.text: Ask the course office about an accountancy apprenticeship route
Try one AI tool slowly on a single assignment
Keep the Saturday and Sunday bakery shifts
Talk to Dad and my tutor before any big choice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit more reasonable. It would give us time to sort out rules and for businesses to plan. I'd still stay out of arguments about it, because I've got enough to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better than two. I'd graduate, maybe do two years in a job, and then it would arrive. I'd still be worried, because I'm not fast, but I'd have time to catch up. My main worry is not being ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, but I'd choose modules in finance and operations, the parts where people check and decide. I'd learn one AI tool in my second year, and another in my third. I'd save every summer wage, and work the placement year at a firm that could keep me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. There's room to breathe. I can plan one year at a time, which is how I like to do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years puts you graduating in 2029. How does that change your thinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you can't stop it, so take small steps. If I'm honest, I'd say it to myself too. I'd tell them I'm not enthusiastic, but I'd rather be ready than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone who says it's all coming too fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ask what you actually need to learn, and learn that. One thing at a time, with someone you trust. That's how I'd manage, so it's how I'd advise someone else.

say: I'd say five years is **more reasonable**, with time for rules and business plans.
I'd stay out of arguments about it because I have enough to do.
think: I'd graduate, work **two years**, and then it arrives, and I'm not fast.
My main worry is **not being ready**.
do: Choose **finance and operations** modules, where people check and decide.
Learn **one AI tool** in second year and another in third.
Save every **summer wage** and take a placement at a firm that could keep me.
feel: **Calmer**: there's room to breathe, and I can plan one year at a time.
S3.quote: I can plan one year at a time, which is how I like to do things.
fieldNote: She needs **small, slow steps** and gets them with five years.
Wants a firm that could keep her after placement, and sees loyalty as a strategy.
Would rather give quiet advice than public opinions.

steps.text: Pick finance and operations modules for second year
Learn one AI tool in second year and another in third
Save every summer wage in a separate account
Take a placement year at a firm that could hire me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a good amount of time. A decade is enough to adapt for most people, if they start sensibly. I'd say we should teach it in school, in a plain way, so no one is left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight and settled somewhere. Ten years is long enough that I won't panic, which for me is a lot. I'd still worry for my dad, who'll be retired, and about house prices, but I'd feel I have a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, get a first job, and slowly learn the tools as my employer asks me to. I'd save for a deposit for a small flat and make sure Dad has what he needs for retirement. And I'd still work some weekends at the bakery, if Mrs Hartley would have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'd even feel a bit hopeful. If I can take it slowly, I think I'd manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still pick the same degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, but I'd add some practical training. I'd still want a job where people matter more than programs, like a small firm, or a family business. A big firm would probably replace me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you if you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waiting until it happens to me. I know that's my habit. I'd have to learn that waiting isn't the same as being careful, and I'd start something small now, before I'm forced to.

say: I'd say a **decade** is enough for most people to adapt, if they start sensibly.
I'd say we should teach it in school, in plain words.
think: Ten years is long enough that I **won't panic**, which for me is a lot.
I'd still worry about **my dad** in retirement and house prices.
do: Finish the degree, get a first job and learn **tools** as my employer asks.
Save a **deposit** for a small flat.
Make sure Dad has what he needs in **retirement**.
feel: Fairly **calm**, even a little hopeful, if I can take it slowly.
S4.quote: I'd have to learn that waiting isn't the same as being careful, and I'd start something small now, before I'm forced to.
fieldNote: She admits her habit of **waiting** may be a risk of its own.
Ten years shifts her focus to a deposit and her father's retirement.
Prefers a small firm, where she is known, over a big employer.

steps.text: Save for a deposit on a small flat
Set aside money for Dad's retirement
Learn the tools when my first employer asks
Keep working some weekends at the bakery

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm slow to change and I'd have debt and nothing to show. What would help is slow, patient training with a real person next to me, honest advice from the university, and some way to pay my loan if the jobs aren't there.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: No, only that I'm not against the tools, I'm just slow to trust them. If someone I know shows me, I'll try. It's strangers that make me nervous.

headlineQuote: My marks are mine, and I'd never want a tutor to ask how I wrote something and not know.
portrait: Amira is an **18-year-old** business student who lost her mother at fourteen and lives with her electrician dad.
She works at a **bakery** on weekends, avoids AI tools and likes small, careful steps.
She is **anxious** in most scenarios and alarmed when AGI is two years away, with her dad's safety on her mind.
Ten years makes her calm, though she admits she tends to **wait** too long.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: her course might be worthless before she finishes, with debt on her dad's household.
whatWouldHelp: **Patient training** beside a real person, honest advice from the university, and loan relief if jobs aren't there.
